newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - market loaded but may retrace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - market loaded but may retrace.

text.p: U.S. crude oil markets remain overburdened with supply, but outright prices should retrace a portion of the extreme losses pegged last week, according to analysts and traders Monday.
Market direction will depend heavily on what happens when and if prompt futures re-test vital technical support from $18.80 to $19.00 a barrel.
"It will probably come down and take a look at $19.00, but hold those levels and start a modest recovery," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
Monday trading has so far played out the recovery scenario, though gains are a mere drop in the bucket when compared to last week's declines.
At 1520 GMT, May West Texas Intermediate/Cushing was around 35 cents firmer at $19.40-50 a barrel, but held a 10 cents discount to June WTI/Cushing.
Technical numbers aside, most market watchers forecast continued pressure on prices from fundamental bearishness, though even that play may be overdone according to some.

More bearish traders simply point to the fact Shell Oil is offering at least one or two North Sea Brent cargoes in the U.S. Gulf, after the company devoured eight North Sea Brent cargoes last week from British Petroleum.
Shell was offering the Brents for the first 10 days in May at May WTI minus $1.10, a price called reasonable by one trader, at least in current market conditions.
Those conditions have left domestic crudes in the lurch, with Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James hovering around a 40 cts discount to the benchmark.
"That (Shell) Brent crude will probably end up in Capline since the price for it is way better than for LLS," said a Texas trader.
Capline is the major pipeline artery running from the U.S. Gulf Coast to the Midwest, with capacity to move 1.1 million barrels per day (bpd) through its system.
Still, there is not more room for LLS deflation, with some cash dealers saying the limit to a discount is seen around the 45-50 cts level.
On the sour side of business, seasonal support for West Texas Sour/Midland has not materialized, leaving WTS at $2.40-50 under the WTI marker.

Displaced crudes in the Mediterranean -- as a result of renewed Iraqi exports under the U.N. oil deal -- have combined with Latin American and Canadian deliveries to depress prices, traders in the U.S. Gulf said.
But further price declines are expected, some analysts see the market stabilizing for now.
"Three to four weeks from now you should see higher prices," Brown said, saying he expected a true $18.00 a barrel market sometime in the third or fourth quarter but not now.

Traders said this week should bring no drastic change in market contango, whereby prompt-delivery crude is at a discount to forward-delivery. The front-month May contract was about five cents below June futures in mid-morning trading Monday.
"If a recovery is led by refiner demand then we should see a flattening (of the contango) to slight backwardation," Brown said.
Traders said direction will also be influenced by weekly inventory data, notably where imports stand in Tuesday's American Petroleum Institute (API) report.
API numbers last week showed imports sharply higher from the previous measure at 8.02 million bpd.
--Patrick Connole, New York Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
